title: The Unphotocopiable Bit
question: Why can't a qubit be copied, and how do engineers use that?
hook: The same rule that makes quantum data impossible to duplicate also makes it hard to spy on.
idea: Measuring a quantum system changes it, which limits copying but lets engineers build communication where interception shows.

beats.prompt: A spy taps the light carrying a quantum key between two offices and tries to read it. What happens?

choices.label: The interception becomes obvious to the offices
Nothing changes, since reading light leaves no trace
choices.feedback: This is how ordinary taps work, but a quantum transmission is built so that interception shows.

choices.label: The key grows stronger because it was read
choices.feedback: Reading does not strengthen anything; it disturbs the transmission.

beats.explain: Quantum key distribution transmits information in a way that makes any interception obvious to the user.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: A qubit can be 1, 0, or any superposition of them.
Measuring a quantum system changes it.
So measure a qubit many times to build perfect backups.
That is why a qubit cannot be copied.
beats.explain: Because measuring changes the system, repeated measuring cannot give backups; that is exactly why copying fails.

beats.prompt: match each tool to what it does
pairs: Imitates a real-world system such as a chemical compound
Moves a qubit's state without sending the particle
beats.explain: Each tool uses a quantum feature for a different job.
The first three are techniques for quantum secure communication; the others are things quantum computers are expected to run.
